marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q019.takeaway: Thyroxine generally raises glucose availability/production; it is incorrectly paired with a decrease in blood glucose.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q019.displayText:
Thyroxine generally raises glucose availability/production; it is incorrectly paired with a decrease in blood glucose.

The incorrect pair is thyroxine - decreased blood glucose. Thyroxine is a diabetogenic hormone leading to an increase in blood glucose levels.
Effects of hormones on carbohydrate metabolism:
• Catecholamines: Activation of glycogen phosphorylase and therefore glycogenolysis occurs. Hepatic glucose output is increased, producing hyperglycemia.
• Glucocorticoids: Glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex elevate blood glucose by stimulating gluconeogenesis and inhibiting glucose utilization by the cells.
• Growth hormone: The effects of growth hormone are partly direct and partly mediated via IGF-I (Insulin-like Growth Factor-I). The growth hormone mobilizes FFA from adipose tissue, thus favoring ketogenesis. It decreases glucose uptake into some tissues (“anti-insulin action”), increases hepatic glucose output, and may decrease tissue binding of insulin.
Note: Infusing catecholamine (epinephrine) mainly promotes glycogenolysis and it is also associated with enhanced rates of aerobic glycolysis in skeletal muscles during exercise (resulting in adenosine triphosphate production).
emphasis: Thyroxine generally raises glucose availability/production; it is incorrectly paired with a decrease in blood glucose

rationales.a: Epinephrine stimulates glycogenolysis and glycolysis, increasing glucose availability.
rationales.b: Insulin promotes protein synthesis and anabolism.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q020.takeaway: Amino acids stimulate both insulin and glucagon after a protein-rich low-carbohydrate meal, preventing hypoglycemia.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q020.displayText:
Amino acids stimulate both insulin and glucagon after a protein-rich low-carbohydrate meal, preventing hypoglycemia.

A meal rich in arginine and alanine stimulates both insulin and glucagon secretion. Hence,
hypoglycemia does not occur.
Increased blood amino acids stimulate secretion of glucagon, which in turn causes the amino
acids to get converted to glucose. So, the mechanism by which hypoglycemia is prevented after a
protein rich meal is secretion of glucagon.
emphasis: Amino acids stimulate both insulin and glucagon after a protein-rich low-carbohydrate meal, preventing hypoglycemia

rationales.a: Cortisol is not the immediate meal-linked safeguard against insulin-induced hypoglycemia.
rationales.c: Amino acids do not promptly become glucose in a way that fully explains the protection.
rationales.d: Amino acids do not prevent insulin-receptor binding; glucagon counterbalances insulin.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q021.takeaway: After beta-cell destruction, insulin deficiency promotes proteolysis and raises plasma amino acids; a fall in amino acids is least likely.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q021.displayText:
After beta-cell destruction, insulin deficiency promotes proteolysis and raises plasma amino acids; a fall in amino acids is least likely.

A fall in plasma amino acid concentration is least likely to be seen in this case.
Injury to the beta cells of the pancreas impairs insulin production rendering the rat insulin deficient. Due to insulin deficiency, catabolism of proteins increases and amino acids in plasma increase.
Insulin deficiency increases blood glucose levels, which lead to glycosuria and osmotic diuresis with extracellular dehydration. There is increase in the plasma osmolality.
Insulin deficiency causes increased utilization of fats, excess production of ketoacids and metabolic acidosis. Metabolic acidosis - a rise in the plasma H+ develops.
emphasis: After beta-cell destruction, insulin deficiency promotes proteolysis and raises plasma amino acids; a fall in amino acids is least likely

rationales.a: Insulin deficiency and ketosis can raise hydrogen-ion concentration.
rationales.b: Reduced insulin’s anabolic restraint increases proteolysis and plasma amino acids.
rationales.d: Hyperglycemia and dehydration can raise plasma osmolality.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q022.takeaway: Insulin suppresses hepatic glucose output, including by inhibiting glucose-6-phosphatase expression/activity.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q022.displayText:
Insulin suppresses hepatic glucose output, including by inhibiting glucose-6-phosphatase expression/activity.

Insulin inhibits glucose-6-phosphatase.
Insulin promotes liver uptake, storage, and the use of glucose. After a meal, insulin causes glucose to be rapidly stored in the liver in the form of glycogen. This occurs by:
• Inactivation of liver phosphorylase, which is the principal enzyme that causes liver glycogen to split into glucose.
• Enhanced uptake of glucose by the liver cells by increasing the activity of the enzyme glucokinase which causes phosphorylation of glucose after it enters the liver cells. Once phosphorylated, the glucose is temporarily trapped inside the liver cells because phosphorylated glucose cannot diffuse back through the cell membrane.
• Increased activity of enzymes that promote glycogen synthesis, like glycogen synthase.
When insulin levels drop (Example: fasting), glucose phosphatase gets activated. This causes phosphate to get detached from glucose phosphate, allowing free glucose from the liver cells to re-enter circulation.
emphasis: Insulin suppresses hepatic glucose output, including by inhibiting glucose-6-phosphatase expression/activity

rationales.a: Insulin inhibits glycogen phosphorylase rather than activating it.
rationales.b: Insulin increases glucokinase expression/activity in liver.
rationales.c: Insulin activates glycogen synthase to promote glycogen storage.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q023.takeaway: Diazoxide opens beta-cell ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels, hyperpolarizing the membrane and reducing insulin secretion.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q023.displayText:
Diazoxide opens beta-cell ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels, hyperpolarizing the membrane and reducing insulin secretion.

Diazoxide acts by opening ATP sensitive K+ channels and causing a decrease in insulin secretion.
Glucose enters beta cells of the pancreas via GLUT-2 receptors. Once inside, it is phosphorylated by glucokinase (rate-limiting step) to glucose-6-phosphate which is oxidized to form adenosine triphosphate (ATP). This ATP causes closure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels and hence depolarization. This leads to opening voltage-gated calcium channels and Ca2+ influx. This stimulates fusion of the insulin-containing vesicles with the cell membrane and secretion of insulin into the extracellular fluid by exocytosis.
Diazoxide keeps the ATP sensitive K+ channels open and prevents depolarization and subsequent insulin release.
Sulfonylureas cause closure of the ATP sensitive K+ channels, leading to increased insulin secretion.
emphasis: Diazoxide opens beta-cell ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels, hyperpolarizing the membrane and reducing insulin secretion

rationales.b: KATP closure depolarizes the beta cell and increases insulin secretion, opposite diazoxide.
rationales.c: Diazoxide does not act by increasing GLUT4 abundance.
rationales.d: Opening voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels would promote insulin release, opposite diazoxide.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q024.takeaway: Severe neuroglycopenia and coma may occur when blood glucose falls below about 30 mg/dL.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q024.displayText:
Severe neuroglycopenia and coma may occur when blood glucose falls below about 30 mg/dL.

Coma occurs when glucose levels fall below 30 mg/dL.
emphasis: Severe neuroglycopenia and coma may occur when blood glucose falls below about 30 mg/dL

rationales.b: 45 mg/dL is low and symptomatic but is above the severe coma threshold in the source item.
rationales.c: 15 mg/dL is more severe than the stated threshold.
rationales.d: 5 mg/dL is far below the level at which coma may occur.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q025.takeaway: Insulin signals through a receptor tyrosine kinase with intrinsic kinase activity.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH38_Q025.displayText:
Insulin signals through a receptor tyrosine kinase with intrinsic kinase activity.

Insulin uses the receptor tyrosine kinase signalling to exert its functions.
Other hormones acting in a similar fashion includes:
• Growth hormone
• Growth factors like VEGF, PDGF, FGF, NGF
emphasis: Insulin signals through a receptor tyrosine kinase with intrinsic kinase activity

rationales.b: TSH signals through a G-protein-coupled receptor, mainly Gs/cAMP.
rationales.c: TRH signals through a Gq-coupled receptor, not a receptor tyrosine kinase.
rationales.d: MSH acts through melanocortin GPCRs rather than receptor tyrosine kinase.
